no-tipping.title: No Tipping Needed
no-tipping.subtitle: Service is included — just pay the bill.
body: Tipping is not a custom in mainland China. Restaurants, taxis, and hotels do not expect a tip, and in most places there is no tip line on the bill at all.
Service charges are already built into the prices you pay, so leaving extra money is unnecessary and can even be awkward. If you insist, staff may chase you to return the change.
The closest thing to tipping is rounding up small change or leaving loose coins, but even that is optional and rarely expected.
In high-end hotels, a porter may accept a small note politely, but you are never obligated. Foreign tourists sometimes tip out of habit — locals simply say 谢谢 and move on.
The rule of thumb: pay the amount on the bill, smile, and say 谢谢 (xiè xie).
no-tipping.tip: Don't worry about tipping — just pay the bill and say 谢谢 (xiè xie).

phrases.en: Thank you, but I don't need a tip.
I'll just pay the bill as it is.

chi-le-ma.title: "Have You Eaten?" as a Greeting
chi-le-ma.subtitle: 吃了吗 is hello, not a dinner invitation.
body: 吃了吗？ (chī le ma?) literally means 'Have you eaten?' but in most situations it is just a casual hello, similar to saying 'How are you?' in English.

People use it when bumping into neighbors or friends near meal times, especially around lunch or dinner. You do not need to actually be hungry — a simple '吃了，你呢？' (Yes, and you?) is the natural reply.
It comes from a tradition where food was not always guaranteed, so asking if someone had eaten showed real care. Today it is a polite, warm way of acknowledging someone.
Do not worry that the person is inviting you to a meal. A real invitation will usually add specifics, like 去吃饭吧 or 一起吃点东西.
The safest answer is '吃了，谢谢！你呢？' (Yes, thanks! And you?), even if you have not actually eaten.
chi-le-ma.tip: Treat 吃了吗 as a greeting, not an invitation — just smile, answer, and ask back.

tea-tap.title: The Tea Table Knock
tea-tap.subtitle: Tap two fingers to say thank you for tea.
body: When someone pours tea for you, tapping two fingers gently on the table a few times is a quiet way to say thank you, especially in southern China and Cantonese settings.
The custom is said to come from an old story where an emperor's servant could not bow openly, so he tapped his fingers to resemble a kneeling gesture.
How to do it: use your index and middle finger together and tap lightly two or three times. It is optional, but it is a nice touch with tea-drinking hosts.
Younger people may just nod and say 谢谢. In formal business meals, doing it correctly is appreciated by older guests.
Never tap loudly or rhythmically — the whole point is a quiet, subtle thanks that does not interrupt the conversation.
tea-tap.tip: When tea is poured, lightly tap two fingers on the table as a quiet 'thank you'.

slurping.title: Making Sounds While Eating
slurping.subtitle: Soft noodle-slurping is fine in China.
body: In many parts of China, especially the south, making soft sounds while eating noodles or soup is not considered rude. It is sometimes even taken as a sign that you enjoy the food.
Unlike Western etiquette, where quietness at the table is ideal, slurping up hot noodles quickly helps cool them down and is common in noodle shops.
That said, loud smacking of the lips, talking with a full mouth, or reaching across others' plates is still considered bad manners in most homes and restaurants.
It is fine to slurp noodles softly; what matters more is saying 好吃 (hǎo chī, delicious) and thanking the host or cook.
When in doubt, follow the locals around you — casual street shops are relaxed, while formal banquets call for quieter table manners.
slurping.tip: Soft noodle-slurping is fine; just avoid loud lip-smacking and talking with a full mouth.

personal-space.title: Personal Space in Crowded China
personal-space.subtitle: Queues and contacts are closer than you may expect.
body: Chinese cities are densely populated, so personal space is naturally smaller than in many Western countries. In queues, buses, or subways, people may stand closer and light body contact is common without bad intentions.
Queue-jumping is generally frowned upon, but pushing onto a crowded train or bus during rush hour is expected rather than aggressive.
When taking group photos, strangers may step into your frame or stand very near — this is usually curiosity, not intrusion.
It helps to stay calm and not take closeness personally. Saying 不好意思 politely if someone bumps you is enough; an angry reaction surprises most people.
If you need space, a calm '请让一下' (qǐng ràng yí xià, please let me through) works well.
personal-space.tip: Don't take close queues or accidental contact personally; a polite 请让一下 works.

queue-etiquette.title: Queue Etiquette: First Come, First Served
queue-etiquette.subtitle: Line up and take a number — jostling is frowned upon.
body: Chinese cities are crowded, but queues are taken seriously. At bank counters, ticket windows, hospitals, and many restaurants, people take a numbered ticket and wait for their turn rather than forming a loose line.
The rule is simple: first come, first served (先来后到). Cutting in line is widely criticized, and locals may call it out directly if someone tries.
During security checks at subway stations, airports, or major landmarks, expect organized queues and patience. Keep your bag ready and follow the staff's instructions.
That said, on rush-hour buses and trains, personal space is tight and a gentle push to board is normal — this is not rudeness, just practical density.
If you are unsure where the line starts, watch others or ask: 请问，队排在哪儿？(Qǐng wèn, duì pái zài nǎr?)
queue-etiquette.tip: Take a numbered ticket where given; never cut in line, and ask politely where the queue starts.

phrases.en: Excuse me, where is the line?

seat-priority.title: Offering Your Seat
seat-priority.subtitle: Give up your seat to elders, pregnant women, and people with children.
body: On buses and the subway in China, giving your seat to elderly people, pregnant women, women holding babies, and people with small children is a strong social norm, usually expected of young passengers.
Priority seats (爱心座) are marked near the doors; even in regular seats, standing up and waving someone over is common.
The gesture is usually silent — just stand up, gesture toward the seat, and the person will thank you. If they decline, a smile and 没关系 is enough.
Young people sitting while an elder stands nearby can draw looks of disapproval. Foreign visitors who offer a seat often get warm smiles in return.
If you are carrying a heavy bag or are clearly tired, it is also fine to keep your seat — the norm is about consideration, not obligation.
seat-priority.tip: Offer your seat to elders, pregnant women, or people with small children on buses and the subway.

phrases.py: Méiguānxi, wǒ xià yī zhàn jiù dào.
phrases.en: It's okay, I'll get off at the next stop.

weather-smalltalk.title: Weather as Small Talk
weather-smalltalk.subtitle: Comments on the weather open everyday conversations.
body: Like in many countries, weather is the safest small talk in China. 今天天气真好！ (What a nice day!) or 今天真冷 (It's really cold today) are common greetings between acquaintances.
When rain or strong sun is expected, locals often advise each other: 明天要下雨，带把伞 (It may rain tomorrow, bring an umbrella).
In winter, northerners talk about heating and how cold it is; in southern cities, summer humidity and the long rainy season are common topics.
These comments are not a request for a forecast — a short agreement or thanks is enough: 是啊，今天太热了 (Yeah, it's too hot today).
Accepting a practical tip, like 记得带伞 (remember to bring an umbrella), is part of the care that runs through everyday conversation.
weather-smalltalk.tip: Reply to weather small talk with a short agreement, and bring an umbrella when warned about rain.

phrases.en: The weather is so nice today!

phrases.py: Yào xià yǔ le, dài bǎ sǎn ba.
phrases.en: It's going to rain, bring an umbrella.

smoking-rules.title: Smoking Rules Indoors
smoking-rules.subtitle: Most indoor public places are smoke-free.
body: Since 2011, China has had a national ban on smoking in indoor public places such as restaurants, hotels, offices, and public transport. Many cities, including Beijing and Shanghai, have even stricter local rules.
You will see designated smoking areas (吸烟区), usually outdoors or in ventilated zones at stations, airports, and some hotels.
Asking a stranger not to smoke is less common than in some Western countries, but lighting up indoors where others can smell it draws clear disapproval.
If you are a guest, smoking in someone's home without asking is impolite — step outside and ask first.
Secondhand smoke is a real concern in daily life; a polite 请问这里可以抽烟吗？ gets you the answer before you light up.
smoking-rules.tip: Smoke only in designated outdoor areas, and ask before lighting up anywhere indoors.

phrases.zh: 不好意思，这里不能吸烟。
phrases.en: I'm sorry, smoking is not allowed here.

phrases.py: Máfan nín bǎ yān miè le.
phrases.en: Could you please put out your cigarette?

hot-water.title: Hot Water, Not Cold · 喝热水
hot-water.subtitle: Why everyone carries a thermos.
body: In China, drinking hot or warm water is the default, and many people believe cold water is hard on the stomach, especially after meals or during a period. Restaurants hand you hot water or tea before you even order, and insulated thermoses are everywhere.
You'll see hot-water dispensers in offices, stations, hotels and even on trains. Fill your own bottle for free rather than buying cold drinks.
If you prefer cold water, just ask — most cafes and convenience stores sell chilled bottled water, and younger Chinese are increasingly comfortable with it.
hot-water.tip: When handed a cup of hot water, accept it with a smile; it signals care, not an odd choice.

phrases.py: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī bēi wēnshuǐ.
phrases.en: A glass of warm water, please.
I am used to drinking cold water.

midday-nap.title: The Midday Nap · 午睡
midday-nap.subtitle: Why China quiets down after lunch.
body: Many Chinese schools and offices build in a short rest after lunch, and napping at one's desk or even dozing on public transport is common and socially accepted rather than seen as lazy.

The habit reflects the traditional idea of recharging energy (养生, yǎngshēng) and the practical reality of long school and work days. You may see students resting their heads on folded arms for twenty minutes after the noon meal.
Don't wake someone sleeping in a shared space unless necessary; it's considered considerate to let them rest and keep noise low.
midday-nap.tip: Keep your voice down between roughly 1 and 2 p.m. in offices and dormitories — it's quiet time.

phrases.en: I'm going to take a nap.
I will rest for half an hour at noon.
Keep your voice down, he's taking a nap.

pajamas-outside.title: Pajamas Outside · 穿睡衣下楼
pajamas-outside.subtitle: Loungewear on the evening stroll.
body: In many neighborhoods, especially older residential compounds, people step out in the evening in comfortable pajama-style loungewear to walk the dog, grab a snack or take out the trash. It's a relaxed, neighborhood-life habit rather than a fashion statement.
It's most common within one's own community (小区) in the evening; people generally change before going to work, to a mall or to a formal place.
As a visitor you don't need to copy it, but don't be surprised or assume someone is ill — it simply means they feel at home in their neighborhood.
pajamas-outside.tip: Loungewear is fine inside your compound; change into street clothes for offices, malls and restaurants.

phrases.en: I'm going downstairs to buy something.
I'm going for a walk in the neighborhood.
It's very lively in the evening.

ac-compromise.title: The Air-Conditioning Compromise · 空调温度
ac-compromise.subtitle: Negotiating the office temperature.
body: Air-conditioning is a frequent topic: many older Chinese worry that strong cold air causes colds, stiff necks or stomach trouble, so offices and restaurants often set it warmer than Western visitors expect, or direct vents away from people.
On trains and in malls it can swing to the opposite extreme and feel very cold. Carrying a light layer is the practical solution.
If the air is blowing directly on you, it's fine to politely ask to adjust the vent or move seats; colleagues will usually accommodate.
ac-compromise.tip: Carry a thin jacket in summer — indoor AC can be far colder than the weather outside.

phrases.en: The air conditioning is a bit cold.

phrases.py: Néng bǎ fēng tiáo xiǎo yīdiǎnr ma?
phrases.en: Could you turn the fan down a bit?

life-on-phone.title: Life on the Phone · 手机生活
life-on-phone.subtitle: How one app runs daily routines.
body: A huge amount of daily life in China happens inside super-apps: messaging, payments, hailing taxis, ordering food, booking trains, checking bus times, sharing bikes and even showing ID. Newcomers often notice how rarely people use cash or cards.

To take part you'll typically want a local phone number, a payment app linked to a bank card or short-term international card, and a translation app. Many services also work through mini-programs inside the main chat app.
It's normal to scan a QR code at a small stall, a parking gate or a vending machine. When unsure, ask staff to show you the code.
life-on-phone.tip: Set up mobile payment and the main chat app early — they unlock most of daily life.

phrases.py: Wǒ sǎo nǐ háishì nǐ sǎo wǒ?
phrases.en: Should I scan you or will you scan me?
Help me connect to the internet.

scan-to-pay.title: Scan to Pay · 扫码支付
scan-to-pay.subtitle: The two ways to pay by QR.
body: QR payment works in two directions: the merchant shows a code for you to scan (扫商家码), or you show your personal payment barcode for them to scan (出示付款码). Small stalls use the first; supermarkets and chains use the second.
Street vendors, market stalls and even musicians performing on the subway often accept QR payment, so carrying some small cash as backup is useful but rarely essential in cities.
Always confirm the amount before approving, and connect only to the shop's official code. If a payment fails, show the screen to staff rather than paying twice.
scan-to-pay.tip: Open your payment barcode at the checkout; for small stalls, scan their printed QR and enter the amount.

phrases.en: Where do I scan the code?

phrases.py: Fù hǎo le, nǐ kàn yīxià.

delivery-express.title: Delivery & Express · 外卖快递
delivery-express.subtitle: Food and parcels at your door in minutes.
body: Food delivery (外卖) and parcel courier (快递) services are extremely fast and cheap, with orders often arriving in under forty minutes. Couriers may call, text or leave items at a pickup station (驿站) or smart locker (快递柜).
When you order, you'll need your address in Chinese and a reachable phone number. Apartment compounds usually have a designated delivery shelf or locker where packages wait for pickup.
Receiving a code by text to open a locker is normal. If you miss a delivery, reply to the courier or use the app to arrange redelivery.
delivery-express.tip: Save your address in Chinese and watch for a locker pickup code by text.

phrases.en: Has the courier left the package at the delivery station?

polite-no.title: The Polite 'No'
polite-no.subtitle: 再说吧 and 下次吧 often mean a soft refusal.
body: A direct 'no' can feel harsh in Chinese culture, so people often decline indirectly. Phrases like 再说吧 (let's talk later), 下次吧 (next time), or 考虑一下 (let me think it over) often mean a soft refusal.
This style keeps things harmonious and saves the other person's face. A vague answer usually hides a real 'no', and pushing for a definite reply can make both sides uncomfortable.
When you invite someone and get 再说吧, it is best to thank them and drop the topic rather than pressing again.
The same goes for offers of food or gifts: the first 不用了 (no need) may be genuine politeness, but repeated insistence is unnecessary unless you know the person well.
Reading these soft refusals prevents awkwardness. If someone truly wants to accept, they will usually agree clearly.
polite-no.tip: Treat 再说吧 / 下次吧 as a gentle 'no' — smile, thank them, and move on.

gift-taboos.title: Gift-Giving Taboos
gift-taboos.subtitle: Avoid clocks, pears, umbrellas, and white wrapping.
body: Gift-giving is common in China, but a few items carry unlucky meanings because their names sound like sad or unwanted words.

A clock (钟, zhōng) sounds like 终 (the end, as in a funeral), so giving a clock is a big no. A pear (梨, lí) sounds like 离 (to separate), and an umbrella (伞, sǎn) sounds like 散 (to split up) — bad for couples or close friends.

Avoid giving green hats (绿帽子) — the phrase means a partner is unfaithful. White is associated with funerals, and the number four (四, sì) sounds like 死 (death), so skip sets of four and white-wrapped gifts.
Safe, welcome gifts: tea, fruit, nice snacks, alcohol, or something from your home country. Red or gold wrapping is considered lucky.
When giving or receiving a gift, use both hands. Gifts are often not opened in front of the giver, unlike in the West.
gift-taboos.tip: Avoid clocks, pears, umbrellas, green hats, and white or sets of four; red wrapping is safe.

phrases.en: Giving a clock as a gift is not appropriate.
How about giving some fruit as a gift?

names.title: Chinese Names and Titles
names.subtitle: Family name first; use 王老师, not a given name.
body: Chinese names put the family name first and the given name second: in 王芳, the family name is 王 and the given name is 芳.
Addressing people respectfully matters. Use a title plus surname — 王老师 (Teacher Wang), 李经理 (Manager Li), 张医生 (Dr. Zhang) — rather than using their given name.
Calling elders or teachers by their given name is considered rude. Younger people and close friends may use given names or nicknames, but wait until you are invited.
Foreigners are often given a friendly Chinese nickname by colleagues; it is a sign of warmth, so accepting it gracefully helps build relationships.
When unsure, use 您 (nín, the polite 'you') with seniors and service staff, and 你 (nǐ) with friends.
names.tip: Family name first; say 王老师 / 李经理, never an elder's given name, and use 您 with seniors.

face.title: The Concept of Face
face.subtitle: 面子 means dignity — keep it for everyone.
body: 面子 (miàn zi), or 'face', means dignity and social reputation. Keeping face for yourself and others is central to daily interactions in China.
Public criticism, blunt correction, or making someone lose an argument in front of others can cause a big loss of face. Even if you are right, say it softly and in private.
Leaving people a graceful 'out' is valued: instead of saying 'you are wrong', use '我觉得可能这样更好' (I think this might be better).
Polite refusals and modest words like 哪里哪里 (it's nothing) often follow compliments. Accept praise with a little humility rather than boasting.
Giving face also means acknowledging status — letting elders or senior colleagues speak first, and thanking your hosts warmly.
face.tip: Never embarrass someone publicly; correct softly and in private, and leave a graceful out.

phrases.en: I think this way is better.

man-zou.title: Saying Goodbye: 慢走
man-zou.subtitle: Hosts say 'walk slowly'; guests reply 'stay'.
body: When you see guests off in China, the host often says 慢走 (màn zǒu), which literally means 'walk slowly' but really means 'take care on your way' or 'safe journey'.
It is a warm, polite phrase, not a comment on your walking speed. Guests usually reply with 留步 (liú bù, 'stay, don't see me out') or just a thank-you and a wave.
Hosts may walk you to the elevator, the doorway, or even the street, and standing a moment after the guest leaves is a sign of respect.
Do not be surprised if hosts keep waving until you disappear around the corner. It shows care, not distrust.
As a visitor, a simple '谢谢，请留步！' back with a smile is perfectly natural and appreciated.
man-zou.tip: Hosts say 慢走 ('take care on the way'); reply 留步 ('stay, don't see me out') or wave thanks.

toast-drinking.title: Toasting and Drinking
toast-drinking.subtitle: Raise your glass with both hands and respect the order.
body: At Chinese banquets, toasting (敬酒) is a ritual. When a senior or host toasts you, stand up, hold your glass with both hands, and clink it below the other person's glass as a sign of respect.
You do not have to finish your drink. 干杯 means 'dry the glass', but 随意 (as you like) is perfectly acceptable, especially when you do not drink alcohol.
Beer and baijiu are common; tea or juice works just as well for toasting. A polite 我以茶代酒 (I'll use tea instead of wine) is widely accepted.
Elders and senior guests are toasted first. Younger people usually wait to be invited or toast in turn rather than starting first.
Getting drunk is not expected. Saying 我酒量不好 (I don't hold my drink well) early prevents pressure later.
toast-drinking.tip: Stand, hold your glass with both hands, clink low, and remember 随意 means you don't have to finish.

phrases.en: I'll toast with tea instead of alcohol.

paying-bill.title: Who Pays the Bill
paying-bill.subtitle: Fighting over the bill is common — but going Dutch is fine too.
body: At meals among friends, colleagues, or relatives, it is normal for people to enthusiastically grab the bill and insist on paying. This 'bill-fighting' (抢买单) is a show of generosity and friendship, not a real conflict.
Hosts often treat guests as a matter of course; if you are the visitor, letting your host pay once is polite rather than rude.
Among young friends, proposing '我们AA吧' (let's split it) or '下次我请' (next time is on me) is increasingly common and completely acceptable.
Refusing a host's offer to pay too strongly can feel ungracious. A thank you and '下次我请' balances things nicely.
Tipping is not involved (see No Tipping); the question is simply who covers the bill.
paying-bill.tip: Expect gentle bill-fighting among hosts; saying '我们AA吧' or '下次我请' works among friends.

senior-respect.title: Respecting Elders
senior-respect.subtitle: Use 您, let elders go first, and look after them.
body: Respect for elders (尊老) runs through Chinese daily life. Using 您 rather than 你 with older people and service staff is the baseline polite form.
Practical gestures matter: let elders enter doors first, offer them seats, help with heavy bags, and address them as 叔叔, 阿姨, 爷爷, or 奶奶 rather than using their names.
At dinners, elders are seated first and served first; waiting for them to start eating is expected.
Asking an older person's age directly is not rude in China (您高寿？ for elders), and they may happily answer.
Foreign visitors who use these small gestures quickly find themselves treated with extra warmth.
senior-respect.tip: Use 您, call elders 叔叔/阿姨/爷爷/奶奶, and let them go first through doors.

privacy-questions.title: Personal Questions as Warmth
privacy-questions.subtitle: Age, income, and marriage questions are curiosity, not rudeness.
body: In China, asking about age, salary, marital status, or whether you have children is often a way of showing care and interest, not an invasion of privacy.
Questions like 你多大了？ (How old are you?), 结婚了吗？ (Are you married?), or 一个月挣多少？ (How much do you earn?) come up between acquaintances, colleagues, and especially elders.
You do not have to answer precisely. A light 还可以 (It's all right) or 差不多吧 (More or less) politely deflects without being cold.
Among close friends these questions are normal; among new business contacts they are usually softened after a meal or two.
Taking offense usually surprises people. A smile and a playful '保密' (It's a secret) works well for sensitive topics.
privacy-questions.tip: Don't treat personal questions as rude — answer briefly or smile and say 保密 (it's a secret).

phrases.en: It's okay, but I'd rather not say.

handshakes-greetings.title: Handshakes & Greetings · 握手问候
handshakes-greetings.subtitle: How Chinese people greet in person.
body: Handshakes are common in business and first meetings, usually lighter and briefer than a firm Western handshake. Among friends, nodding and saying 你好 is enough; close friends may wave rather than hug.
Hugging and cheek-kissing are not standard greetings and can make new acquaintances awkward, especially across age or gender. A warm smile and a slight nod work universally.
Business greetings often begin with a business card and a surname-plus-title, such as 王总 (Manager Wang) or 李老师 (Teacher Li).
handshakes-greetings.tip: Offer a gentle handshake in business settings; a smile and nod cover almost everything else.

phrases.py: Nǐ hǎo, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ.

phrases.en: I've heard a lot about you.

business-cards.title: Exchanging Business Cards · 递名片
business-cards.subtitle: Present and receive with two hands.
body: Business cards are exchanged with care: offer yours with two hands, text facing the receiver so they can read it, and receive theirs the same way. Take a moment to actually read it rather than pocketing it immediately.
Placing a received card on the table in front of you during a meeting shows respect; writing notes on it in front of the person can be seen as careless, so do that later.
Cards matter less among young tech companies, where adding someone on the main chat app is the everyday equivalent.
business-cards.tip: Present and receive cards with two hands and a glance of genuine attention.

phrases.zh: 您的名片能给我一张吗？
phrases.py: Nín de míngpiàn néng gěi wǒ yī zhāng ma?
phrases.en: Could I have one of your business cards?
Let's add each other on WeChat later.

adding-wechat.title: Adding WeChat · 加微信
adding-wechat.subtitle: What swapping contacts really means.
body: Exchanging IDs on the main chat app (加微信) is the everyday way to stay in touch, far more common than asking for a phone number or email. It's a friendly signal after a good conversation, a meeting or even a helpful encounter.
People scan each other's QR codes or search a phone number. Once connected, a short greeting message with your name helps the other person remember who you are.
It's normal for work, friendships and customer service to all happen in the same app, but don't expect an instant reply — many keep groups muted.
adding-wechat.tip: After adding someone, send a quick note with your name so they can label you.

phrases.en: Let's add each other on WeChat.

phrases.py: Nǐ sǎo wǒ háishì wǒ sǎo nǐ?
phrases.en: Should I scan you or will you scan me?

digital-hongbao.title: Digital Red Packets · 发红包
digital-hongbao.subtitle: Lucky money in group chats.
body: Virtual red packets (红包) let people send small amounts of money inside group chats for festivals, birthdays, weddings or simply to liven up a group. A 'lucky money grab' (抢红包), where members race to claim random amounts, is a playful social ritual.
Amounts are usually small and symbolic; the fun is in the grabbing and the good wishes, not the sum. Sending one to a group is a friendly way to celebrate or thank people.
Open a red packet when you see one — leaving it unclaimed is fine, but sending one back later keeps the goodwill balanced. Avoid sending odd or funeral-associated amounts.
digital-hongbao.tip: In group chats, grab red packets for fun and send one back later to keep things even.

phrases.en: Thank you for the boss's red envelope!

table-seating.title: Seating at the Table · 座次
table-seating.subtitle: Where to sit signals respect.
body: At a formal Chinese meal, seating follows hierarchy: the seat facing the door, often with the best view and its back to a wall, is reserved for the host or most senior guest (主宾). Wait to be guided rather than choosing it yourself.
The host typically sits facing the door to manage ordering and serving; guests of honor are placed to the host's right. Round tables and a rotating center make sharing easy.
At casual meals with friends seating is relaxed. When in doubt, pause and let the host gesture you to a seat.
table-seating.tip: At a formal dinner, wait for the host to indicate your seat before sitting.

phrases.en: Please take the seat of honor.

hosting-treat.title: Hosting & Treating · 请客做东
hosting-treat.subtitle: The person who invites usually pays.
body: When someone says 我请客 ('it's my treat'), they mean it — the inviter hosts and pays, and arguing too hard to pay can take away their face. Graciously accept and offer to host the next time instead.
Treating is part of building relationships (人情); favors and meals are reciprocated over time rather than split exactly each time. Among close friends, going Dutch (AA制) is common and easy.
A guest may make a token gesture toward the bill, then let the host win. Repay the gesture later by inviting them out.
hosting-treat.tip: If invited as a guest, accept the treat warmly and plan to host next time.

after-meal-followup.title: After-Meal Follow-Up · 饭后跟进
after-meal-followup.subtitle: A short message closes the loop.
body: After a business meal or a favor, it's thoughtful to send a brief thank-you message later that day or the next, often adding that you arrived home safely (到家了). This small follow-up is valued and keeps the relationship warm.
A typical message thanks the host, mentions the food or a topic you enjoyed, and signals openness to meeting again. It's the digital equivalent of a polite send-off.
Don't let a new contact go cold entirely; an occasional greeting around a festival maintains the connection without pressure.
after-meal-followup.tip: Send a short 'got home safe, thanks' message after a hosted meal.

phrases.en: I'm home, thanks for the hospitality!
We had a great chat today.
Let's meet up again another day.

round-table.title: Round Tables, Shared Dishes · 圆桌合菜
round-table.subtitle: Everyone eats from shared plates.
body: Chinese meals are built around sharing: several dishes are placed in the center and everyone uses chopsticks to take portions into their own bowl of rice. Dishes arrive as they're cooked, not in strict courses.

A good order balances meat, vegetables, soup and a staple, usually with one dish per person plus one more. The host orders for the table and will keep placing good pieces of food into guests' bowls as a sign of care.
Eat a little of everything offered; refusing an entire dish can seem ungracious. You can always say you're full (吃饱了) once you've tried a bite.
round-table.tip: Dishes are shared — take modest portions from the center into your own rice bowl.

lazy-susan.title: The Lazy Susan · 转盘
lazy-susan.subtitle: How to share a big round table.
body: Large round tables have a rotating tray (转盘) in the center so everyone can reach every dish. Turn it slowly, and pause if someone is serving from a plate; never spin it while another person's chopsticks are on it.
A polite host rotates a new dish so that the best piece or the whole fish faces the guest of honor. When tea or soup arrives, you can help pour for those near you before filling your own cup.
Don't reach across others or stand to grab a distant dish — simply rotate the tray until it's within reach.
lazy-susan.tip: Spin the tray gently and stop whenever someone is serving from it.

chopsticks-taboo.title: Chopstick Taboos · 筷子禁忌
chopsticks-taboo.subtitle: A few things never to do.
body: The strongest taboo is sticking chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice, which resembles incense offered to the dead. Also avoid passing food directly from your chopsticks to someone else's, as this echoes a funeral ritual.

Don't tap bowls with chopsticks (associated with begging), point at people with them, or use them to stir dishes around searching for the best piece. Rest them neatly across your bowl or on the rest when not in use.
When served with a spoon for soup or shared dishes, use the communal chopsticks or spoon (公筷) provided for taking food, and your own pair for eating.
chopsticks-taboo.tip: Never stand chopsticks upright in rice; lay them across your bowl or on the rest.

phrases.py: Wǒ bù tài huì yòng kuàizi.
phrases.en: I'm not very good at using chopsticks.

ordering-for-table.title: Ordering for the Table · 点菜
ordering-for-table.subtitle: Balance, variety and the host's role.
body: Ordering is a group decision led by the host, aiming for harmony: a mix of cooking methods, proteins and vegetables, soup, rice or noodles, and usually a whole fish for important meals. Menus often show photos, which makes pointing easy.
Tell the waiter about dietary needs up front — not spicy (不要辣), no cilantro (不要香菜), allergies (过敏). Dishes are shared, so choose a couple of mild options even if you love spice.
It's polite to let the host or most senior person order; if asked for a preference, suggest one dish rather than taking over the whole order.
ordering-for-table.tip: Name your allergies and spice level before ordering; aim for a balanced spread.

rice-vs-noodles.title: Rice vs Noodles · 南米北面
rice-vs-noodles.subtitle: Staples map to the map of China.
body: A rough rule of thumb is 'rice in the south, wheat in the north' (南米北面): southern wet climates favor rice, while the drier north built a cuisine of noodles, steamed buns (包子), dumplings (饺子) and pancakes.
Rice (米饭) is the everyday filler that balances savory dishes; noodles (面) can be a whole meal and symbolize longevity, so long noodles at birthdays are left uncut for a long life.
When eating family-style you order dishes plus a bowl of rice per person; at a noodle shop the noodle bowl itself is the meal.
rice-vs-noodles.tip: Order rice to share with dishes; noodles are usually a complete one-bowl meal.

phrases.en: I'd like a bowl of beef noodles.
Longevity noodles! Wishing you a long life!

regional-cuisines.title: Eight Great Cuisines · 八大菜系
regional-cuisines.subtitle: How regional flavors differ.
body: Chinese cooking is often grouped into major regional cuisines. Sichuan (川) is numbing-spicy from Sichuan peppercorn and chili; Hunan (湘) is hot and smoky; Cantonese (粤) is light, fresh and famous for dim sum; Jiangsu/Zhejiang (苏浙) is sweet and delicate.

Shandong (鲁) favors bold wheat and seafood dishes; Fujian (闽) is light and soupy; Anhui (徽) uses braised mountain ingredients. Northern food leans salty and wheat-based, while the south tends sweeter and rice-based.
Menus often label a dish's origin, so you can travel the country through its food. If you can't handle spice, look for Cantonese, Shanghainese or northern home-style (家常菜) options.
regional-cuisines.tip: Start with mild Cantonese or home-style dishes, then explore Sichuan heat gradually.

phrases.en: I want to eat Sichuan cuisine.

street-food-night-market.title: Street Food & Night Markets · 街头夜市
street-food-night-market.subtitle: Where locals really eat.
body: Night markets (夜市) and snack streets (小吃街) come alive after dark with skewers (烧烤), grilled squid, stinky tofu (臭豆腐), pancakes (煎饼), dumplings, bubble tea and regional specialties. They're cheap, fast and deeply social.
Look for stalls with a crowd and quick turnover — fresh, popular stalls are usually the safest and tastiest. Most items are cooked to order in front of you.
Use your judgment on raw or unpeeled food at very quiet stalls; busy night markets, fruit you peel yourself and hot cooked items are generally safe and delicious.
street-food-night-market.tip: Follow the crowds at busy stalls and choose food cooked hot in front of you.

phrases.en: Stinky tofu smells bad but tastes delicious.

hotpot-etiquette.title: Hotpot Etiquette · 火锅
hotpot-etiquette.subtitle: Cooking together at the table.
body: Hotpot (火锅) is a simmering shared broth in which everyone cooks meat, seafood, tofu, mushrooms and greens. Split pots (鸳鸯锅) offer a mild and a spicy side, a great option if your spice tolerance differs.

Don't dump everything in at once or overcook delicate items; add food in small batches and use the small strainer ladles for items that cook fast. Dip cooked food in your own sesame-oil or sauce mixture.
Drink the cooling broth or soy milk if the spice builds, and never use your personal chopsticks to dig through the shared pot when serving chopsticks are provided.
hotpot-etiquette.tip: Order a split mild-and-spicy pot and cook in small batches.

phrases.en: We'd like a dual-flavor hot pot.

phrases.py: Máodù shuàn jǐ miǎo jiù hǎo.
phrases.en: Mao du (beef tripe) only needs a few seconds to cook.

phrases.py: Tài là le, hē kǒu dòunǎi.
phrases.en: It's too spicy. Have a sip of soy milk.

morning-tea-dimsum.title: Morning Tea & Dim Sum · 早茶点心
morning-tea-dimsum.subtitle: The Cantonese weekend ritual.
body: In Guangdong and Hong Kong, 'morning tea' (早茶/饮茶) is a leisurely weekend meal of small steamed and fried dishes called dim sum (点心): shrimp dumplings (虾饺), soup dumplings (小笼包), rice noodle rolls (肠粉) and custard buns.
Traditionally carts rolled between tables and you pointed at what you wanted; today many places use a paper order sheet or a QR menu. It's meant to be slow — families linger for hours over tea.
Pots of pu'er or jasmine tea are refilled with hot water; tap two fingers on the table when someone pours to say thank you.
morning-tea-dimsum.tip: Dim sum is a slow shared brunch — order a round, sip tea, and add more.

phrases.en: One basket of shrimp dumplings, please.
Waiter, can we get some more water?

tea-culture.title: Tea Culture · 茶文化
tea-culture.subtitle: More than a drink — a sign of welcome.
body: Tea is China's everyday gesture of hospitality: guests are offered tea immediately, and a host keeps the cup topped up. Emptying a whole pot often means it's time to refill; leaving the lid ajar can signal for hot water in some teahouses.

Beyond daily tea, gōngfu tea (功夫茶) is a careful, multi-step way of brewing oolong or pu'er in small clay pots, common in the south. The same leaves are steeped many times, with the first quick rinse poured away.
You don't have to master the ritual. Accept tea with thanks, tap two fingers when poured for, and never fill your own cup first when serving others.
tea-culture.tip: Accept tea as a welcome; when poured for, tap two fingers gently to say thanks.

phrases.en: What kind of tea is this?
Can I get some more water?

baijiu-beer.title: Baijiu, Beer & Toasts · 白酒啤酒
baijiu-beer.subtitle: China's own strong spirit.
body: Baijiu (白酒) is a strong, clear grain spirit served in tiny glasses at banquets, often 50%+ alcohol. It's drunk in toasts rather than sipped casually, and the word 干杯 ('dry cup') can mean bottom's up in a formal setting.

Beer (usually light lager) and tea are common, gentler alternatives. You may toast with beer or tea if you don't drink; what matters is joining the gesture, not the alcohol. Pregnant women and non-drinkers are easily excused.
Never pour only for yourself — pour for the table, and let others fill your glass. Turning a glass down firmly but politely (我酒精过敏 / 我以茶代酒) is respected.
baijiu-beer.tip: Join toasts even with tea; pour for others before yourself.

phrases.en: I'll toast with tea instead of alcohol.

phrases.py: Wǒ jiǔjīng guòmǐn, bù néng hē.
phrases.en: I'm allergic to alcohol, I can't drink.

fruit-to-finish.title: Fruit to Finish · 饭后水果
fruit-to-finish.subtitle: The sweet ending without dessert.
body: Many everyday Chinese meals end not with cake but with a plate of fresh-cut fruit — watermelon, oranges, apple or whatever is in season — served in the restaurant or at home to cleanse the palate.
Dessert as a separate sweet course is more of a Western or special-occasion pattern; sweet soups (甜品/糖水) like red bean, sesame paste or mango pomelo sago are popular regional treats instead.
Bringing fruit when visiting someone's home is a classic, safe hostess gift; a nicely presented fruit basket suits almost any occasion.
fruit-to-finish.tip: Expect fresh fruit rather than cake at the end of an ordinary meal.

doggy-bag.title: Taking Leftovers · 打包
doggy-bag.subtitle: Boxing food is normal and encouraged.
body: Asking to pack leftovers (打包) is completely normal and even encouraged in Chinese restaurants, with no embarrassment attached. Staff will bring boxes or bags, and hotpot and large banquets routinely wrap up untouched food.
Ordering generously to show hospitality can leave extras, so packing them avoids waste and is seen as sensible rather than stingy. It's fine to ask even at a nice restaurant.
Sealed takeout boxes travel well if you're heading home; just carry saucy dishes upright.
doggy-bag.tip: Don't leave a feast untouched — ask 请打包 and box the extras.

halal-vegetarian.title: Halal & Vegetarian Food · 清真素食
halal-vegetarian.subtitle: Finding food that fits your diet.
body: Halal (清真) restaurants run by Hui and other Muslim communities are widespread, marked by the Arabic-style 清真 sign; they serve beef and lamb noodles, buns and grilled skewers with no pork or alcohol. Look for them near mosques and in northwest-cuisine spots.

Vegetarian dining is easiest at Buddhist vegetarian restaurants (素食馆), which often make clever meat-free versions of classic dishes, and at temples. Otherwise, say 我吃素 ('I eat vegetarian') and watch for hidden meat stocks and lard.
Strict vegans should note that dairy is less common but eggs and oyster sauce frequently appear; apps and photos help confirm ingredients.
halal-vegetarian.tip: Look for 清真 for halal and 素食馆 for vegetarian; state your needs clearly.

phrases.en: No meat, onions, or garlic, please.

spring-festival.title: Spring Festival · 春节
spring-festival.subtitle: China's biggest family holiday.
body: Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) is the most important holiday, following the lunar calendar and falling in late January or February. It centers on family reunion, much like Christmas and Thanksgiving combined: cities empty as people travel home.

Homes are cleaned to sweep away bad luck, decorated in red with paper-cuttings and couplets, and doors often bear the character 福 (fú, fortune) upside down, because 'upside-down fortune' sounds like 'fortune has arrived'.
Festivities last about a week to fifteen days, ending with the Lantern Festival. Fireworks (where permitted), lion dances, dumplings in the north and rice cakes in the south all mark the new year.
spring-festival.tip: Expect closures and crowded travel around New Year; greet people with 新年快乐 or 恭喜发财.

chunyun.title: The Spring Rush · 春运
chunyun.subtitle: The largest annual migration on Earth.
body: 春运 (chūnyùn) is the travel rush around Spring Festival, when hundreds of millions of people return to their hometowns and then head back to work. Train and plane tickets sell out weeks ahead, and trains run packed.

If you're in China during this window, book long-distance travel as early as possible and carry your passport, as real-name ticketing is enforced. Many migrant workers make journeys of 20+ hours by train to be home for New Year's Eve.
Big cities can feel unusually quiet during the holiday itself as migrant populations leave, while hometowns and tourist spots become crowded.
chunyun.tip: Book travel far ahead during 春运 and always carry your passport for real-name tickets.

phrases.en: I'm going home for the New Year.
The Spring Festival travel rush is really crowded.

reunion-dinner.title: New Year's Eve Dinner · 年夜饭
reunion-dinner.subtitle: The year's most important meal.
body: The reunion dinner (年夜饭) on New Year's Eve is the emotional heart of the holiday, with generations gathering for a lavish spread. Dishes carry lucky meanings: fish (鱼 yú) sounds like 'surplus', so a whole fish represents abundance and is often left partly uneaten for 'surplus in the new year'.

Dumplings (饺子) shaped like ancient gold ingots symbolize wealth in the north; sweet rice balls (汤圆) signal family togetherness; long uncut noodles mean long life. Red dates, peanuts and seeds appear for prosperity and fertility.
Even family members who cannot attend are symbolically acknowledged, and the meal is followed by staying up late (守岁), watching the New Year gala and setting off firecrackers at midnight.
reunion-dinner.tip: If invited to a reunion dinner, accept warmly — it's a sign you're treated like family.

phrases.en: The New Year's Eve dinner is so lavish!
May you have abundance every year!

lucky-money.title: Lucky Money · 压岁钱
lucky-money.subtitle: Red envelopes for the new year.
body: During Spring Festival, elders and married relatives give children red envelopes (红包/压岁钱) containing fresh banknotes for good luck and protection. The amounts often use lucky numbers and are always even, never 4.

Adults now also send digital red packets in group chats. Recipients traditionally politely decline once or twice before accepting with both hands and good wishes — a show of modesty rather than greed.
If you're a working adult visiting a friend's family, giving a modest red envelope to the children (ask your friend the right amount) is a thoughtful, appreciated gesture.
lucky-money.tip: Give even, lucky sums; recipients should modestly decline once before accepting.

phrases.en: Thank you, and wishing you prosperity!

couplets-fu.title: Couplets & the Fu Character · 春联福字
couplets-fu.subtitle: Red paper wishes on every door.
body: Before New Year, families paste spring couplets (春联) — pairs of poetic lines on red paper — on either side of the door, and a square 福 (fú, fortune) character in the middle or on windows. Red symbolizes luck and wards off a legendary beast.
The 福 character is often pasted upside down on purpose: 福倒了 (fú dào le, fu is upside down) is a pun on 福到了 (fú dào le, fortune has arrived).
Paper-cuttings (窗花) of flowers, animals and the year's zodiac animal decorate windows. Seeing the city turn red overnight is one of the visual joys of the season.
couplets-fu.tip: Paste 福 upside down for the pun 'fortune has arrived'.

phrases.en: Putting up the Spring Festival couplets.
What's the zodiac animal for this year?

lantern-festival.title: Lantern Festival · 元宵节
lantern-festival.subtitle: The bright end of New Year.
body: The Lantern Festival (元宵节) closes the New Year celebrations on the 15th day of the first lunar month with lantern displays, riddle games (猜灯谜), lion dances and the first full moon of the year.
The food is 汤圆 (tāngyuán) or 元宵 — sweet glutinous rice balls in soup, whose round shape and name echo 团圆 (tuányuán), family reunion.
In some cities there are lantern fairs and fireworks; carrying or viewing lanterns is especially beloved by children.
lantern-festival.tip: Eat sweet rice balls and, if there's a fair, try solving a lantern riddle.

phrases.en: What's the answer to this lantern riddle?

qingming.title: Tomb-Sweeping Day · 清明节
qingming.subtitle: Remembering ancestors in spring.
body: Qingming (清明节), usually around April 4–6, is when families tend ancestors' graves, sweep tombs, offer food and flowers, and burn incense or paper offerings. It's a day of remembrance mixed with spring outings, hence its other name, 'Clear and Bright'.
Many people now lay fresh flowers instead of burning paper, especially in cities with fire restrictions. It's also traditional to eat sweet green rice cakes (青团) colored with mugwort.
The holiday coincides with gentle spring weather, so outings, kite-flying and walks in the countryside are common alongside the solemn visits.
qingming.tip: Expect quiet cemetery visits and green 青团 cakes; treat grave sites with respect.

phrases.en: We visit the graves during Qingming.

dragon-boat.title: Dragon Boat Festival · 端午节
dragon-boat.subtitle: Racing boats and sticky rice.
body: The Dragon Boat Festival (端午节), on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month (usually June), honors the ancient poet Qu Yuan with dragon boat races and the eating of zongzi (粽子) — sticky rice wrapped in bamboo or reed leaves.
Zongzi come sweet (red bean, date) in the north and savory (pork, salted egg yolk) in the south. Families hang mugwort and calamus on doors and children may wear colorful silk threads for protection.
Dragon boat races feature paddlers rowing in sync to loud drums; watching one near a river is a highlight of the holiday.
dragon-boat.tip: Try a zongzi and catch a dragon boat race if you're near water.

phrases.en: Do you eat sweet or savory zongzi?

mid-autumn.title: Mid-Autumn Festival · 中秋节
mid-autumn.subtitle: Mooncakes and the fullest moon.
body: Mid-Autumn (中秋节), on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month (around September), is the second-largest family festival after Spring Festival. Families gather to admire the brightest full moon and eat mooncakes (月饼).

Mooncakes are round pastries symbolizing reunion, with fillings like lotus seed paste and salted egg yolk (the yolk represents the moon), red bean, five-nut, or modern snow-skin and ice-cream versions.
People give boxes of mooncakes to relatives, colleagues and clients, and children carry colorful lanterns. It's a time for poems about homesickness and the moon.
mid-autumn.tip: Share mooncakes and look at the full moon; gift a box to your host or colleagues.

phrases.en: Flowers are in full bloom, and the moon is full.
Let's enjoy the moon and eat mooncakes together.

singles-day.title: Singles' Day · 双十一
singles-day.subtitle: The world's biggest shopping festival.
body: November 11 (双十一, 11.11) began playfully as Singles' Day because the date is full of 'ones' representing single people, and e-commerce platforms turned it into the world's largest online shopping event, far bigger than Black Friday.
Retailers offer steep discounts, pre-sale deposits and coupons in the weeks before; packages flood delivery networks for days afterward. Similar smaller sales run on June 18 (618).
It's lighthearted rather than traditional — many couples and families shop the sales too. Set a budget, as countdown deals and stacking coupons are designed to encourage impulse buying.
singles-day.tip: Watch for pre-sale coupons in early November if you want the real discounts.

phrases.en: What did you buy on Singles' Day?
The discounts make it a great deal.
The delivery warehouses are about to overflow.

golden-week.title: Golden Week Holidays · 黄金周
golden-week.subtitle: When the whole country travels.
body: China designates two week-long 'Golden Weeks' — around National Day (Oct 1) and Spring Festival — plus shorter holidays for other festivals, often rearranged with makeup workdays to create continuous breaks.
National Day (国庆节) celebrates the founding of the PRC with flags, flowers and, in milestone years, parades. Scenic spots, trains and highways become extraordinarily crowded during Golden Week.
If you can, travel just before or after the peak, or stay in the city and enjoy a quieter local experience. Book tickets and hotels weeks ahead if you must travel.
golden-week.tip: Avoid major scenic spots during Golden Week itself; book everything early if you go.

phrases.en: Where are you going during Golden Week?

zodiac.title: The Chinese Zodiac · 十二生肖
zodiac.subtitle: Twelve animals, twelve-year cycle.
body: The Chinese zodiac assigns one of twelve animals to each lunar year in a repeating cycle: Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog and Pig. Your animal is said to shape personality and fortune.

One's zodiac year (本命年, běnmìngnián) returns every twelve years and is traditionally considered unlucky, so people wear red underwear, red socks or red bracelets given by elders to ward off misfortune.
The zodiac is a fun, common small-talk topic, and the animal appears on New Year stamps, decorations and gifts. Asking 'What's your sign?' (你属什么?) is an easy conversation starter.
zodiac.tip: In your zodiac year, friends may gift you red items for protection — wear them in good humor.

phrases.en: I was born in the Year of the Dragon.
This year is the Year of the Snake.

visiting-home.title: Visiting a Chinese Home · 上门做客
visiting-home.subtitle: Bring something, take off shoes, be hosted.
body: When invited home, bring a small gift — fruit, tea, quality snacks or something from your country. Arrive close to the agreed time; being very early can catch the host unprepared, while more than 15 minutes late warrants a message.

You'll usually be offered slippers at the door (see the next guide), seated in the best spot, and immediately plied with tea, fruit and snacks. Accept graciously and eat at least a little; refusing everything can seem distant.
Praise the home modestly, avoid sensitive topics, and don't overstay. A thoughtful follow-up message afterward completes the visit.
visiting-home.tip: Bring a small gift, wear presentable socks, and accept the tea and snacks you're offered.

phrases.en: Here's a small gift as a token of my respect.

phrases.py: Bù zǎo le, wǒmen gāi zǒu le.
phrases.en: It's getting late. We should go.

taking-off-shoes.title: Taking Off Shoes · 换鞋
taking-off-shoes.subtitle: Slippers at the door.
body: Many Chinese homes expect shoes to come off at the entrance to keep the floors clean, especially where people sit close to the floor or young children play. Hosts usually offer guest slippers (拖鞋).
Wear clean, hole-free socks on home visits in case slippers aren't offered. Place your shoes neatly with others rather than leaving them scattered.
Some modern households don't mind shoes, so follow the host's cue — if they keep theirs on or wave you in, you can too.
taking-off-shoes.tip: Look for guest slippers and a row of shoes at the door; when in doubt, ask or follow the host.

phrases.en: Should I take off my shoes?

phrases.py: Qǐng jìn qǐng jìn, búyòng huàn xié.
phrases.en: Come in, come in, no need to change shoes.

hosting-guests.title: Hosting Guests · 待客之道
hosting-guests.subtitle: Tea, fruit and constant refills.
body: Chinese hosts show care by feeding and serving guests almost relentlessly — refilling tea, pressing snacks, adding food to your bowl and urging you to eat more (多吃点). This warmth is genuine, not an inconvenience.

A good guest accepts at least some of each offering and expresses enjoyment. You may politely decline after having some; a flat refusal of everything can make the host feel they've failed to welcome you.
When the host pours tea, tap two fingers in thanks; when they refill your rice bowl, hold it slightly with both hands.
hosting-guests.tip: Accept the first offer of tea or food; you can gently decline later once you've had some.

phrases.py: Bié kèqi, jiù dàng zìjǐ jiā.
Wǒ zìjǐ lái, nín bié máng le.
phrases.en: I'll do it myself, don't bother.

banquet-seating.title: Banquet Seating · 宴席座次
banquet-seating.subtitle: Formal dinners have a map.
body: At formal banquets, seating is carefully arranged by rank and relationship. The host takes the seat facing the door (often under a decorative panel), the principal guest sits to the host's right, and other guests are placed outward by seniority.

Wait to be seated rather than choosing a spot, especially at weddings and business banquets, where place cards may be used. The host begins eating and proposes the first toast, after which the meal relaxes.
The guest of honor often receives the first pour of tea or wine and the choicest piece of fish or meat, served with the head or best portion pointing their way.
banquet-seating.tip: At a formal banquet, stand briefly and let the host direct you to your seat.

phrases.py: Nín shì zhǔbīn, qǐng zuò zhè biān.
phrases.en: You're the guest of honor, please sit here.

phrases.py: Wǒ xiān jìng dàjiā yī bēi.
phrases.en: Let me offer a toast to everyone first.

chinese-weddings.title: Chinese Weddings · 婚礼
chinese-weddings.subtitle: Red, banquets and red envelopes.
body: Chinese weddings are festive, with red decorations, photos and often multiple outfits for the couple. The main event is a lavish lunch or dinner banquet (喜酒) of many courses, with the couple and families toasting each table.

Guests typically give a red envelope (红包) rather than a physical gift, containing an even, lucky amount (often ending in 6, 8 or 9, never 4). Sign your name on the envelope so the family can record your gift.
Attire should avoid white (the bride's modern gown aside) and all-black; festive colors are safe. Arrive around the stated time and expect loud music, games and a joyful, crowded hall.
chinese-weddings.tip: Bring a signed red envelope with an even lucky sum and avoid wearing white or all black.

phrases.en: Congratulations and best wishes for a century of happiness!
Wishing you an early birth of a precious child!
Write your name on the red envelope.

funeral-basics.title: Funerals · 葬礼白事
funeral-basics.subtitle: Quiet respect and somber colors.
body: Chinese funerals (白事, 'white affairs') are solemn, family-centered events traditionally involving white or dark clothing, incense, offerings and, depending on region and religion, chanting or a wake. Customs vary widely by area and family.

If attending, dress modestly in black, white or dark colors, avoid bright red and festive jewelry, speak softly, and follow the family's lead in bowing or offering incense. A condolence gift of money in a white or plain envelope is customary in many regions — ask a local friend the local practice and amount.
Do not take photos at the service or of the deceased without explicit permission, and avoid cheerful greetings.
funeral-basics.tip: Wear dark clothing, follow the family's lead, and ask a local friend about the local condolence custom.

phrases.en: May the elderly rest in peace.

phrases.zh: 有什么需要帮忙的尽管说。
phrases.py: Yǒu shénme xūyào bāngmáng de jǐnguǎn shuō.
phrases.en: Feel free to let me know if you need any help.

temple-etiquette.title: Temple Etiquette · 寺庙礼仪
temple-etiquette.subtitle: Visiting Buddhist and Daoist temples.
body: Temples are active places of worship. Dress modestly (cover shoulders and knees), keep your voice low, and silence your phone. Many temples ask visitors to step over door thresholds rather than on them, and to enter using the side rather than the central doorway.

If you watch worshippers, you'll see them light incense, bow three times with hands together, and place the incense in a burner. You may observe quietly without participating; don't stand directly in front of someone praying or photograph them close up.
Photography of statues and the main altar is often prohibited — look for signs or ask. Don't touch relics, drums or bells, and treat monks, nuns and worshippers with respect.
temple-etiquette.tip: Dress modestly, stay quiet, skip photos of altars, and let worshippers practice undisturbed.

phrases.en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

elevators-doors.title: Elevators & Doors · 电梯与门
elevators-doors.subtitle: Let people out before you enter.
body: The standard rule on Chinese subways and elevators is to stand to the side and let exiting passengers out before boarding (先下后上). Holding the elevator for a nearby person is appreciated, and it's common for the person nearest the buttons to press floors for others.
In crowded cities people pack into elevators and trains tightly; personal space shrinks at rush hour without personal intent. A quiet 不好意思 (excuse me) gets you through when leaving.
When someone holds a door or elevator, a nod or 谢谢 is expected; ignoring it reads as slightly cold.
elevators-doors.tip: Let riders out first, stand aside, and press the floor button for others when you're nearest.

phrases.en: Let passengers get off first before boarding.
Excuse me, this is my stop.

phrases.py: Qǐng bāng wǒ àn yīxià wǔ lóu.
phrases.en: Could you please press the fifth floor for me?

bargaining.title: Bargaining at Markets · 讨价还价
bargaining.subtitle: Where and how to negotiate.
body: Bargaining is expected at street markets, tourist stalls, night markets and some small independent shops, but generally not in malls, supermarkets, chain stores or places with clearly printed prices. Keep it light and friendly — it's a game, not a confrontation.

A common approach is to offer well below what you'd happily pay, show mild hesitation, walk away slowly, and let the seller call you back with a lower price. Smiling and paying in cash can help. Once you agree on a price, backing out is poor form.
Don't bargain hard over tiny sums with elderly vendors; the few yuan matter more to them than to you, and goodwill is worth keeping.
bargaining.tip: Bargain playfully at stalls, never at fixed-price chains, and honor a price you agree to.

phrases.zh: 我诚心买，你给个实在价。
phrases.py: Wǒ chéngxīn mǎi, nǐ gěi gè shízài jià.
phrases.en: I'm serious about buying, give me a fair price.

invitations-rsvp.title: Invitations & RSVP · 请客邀约
invitations-rsvp.subtitle: How invites and timing work.
body: Chinese invitations can be indirect and warm — 'let's eat together sometime' (有空一起吃饭) may be a polite pleasantry or a real plan; a specific time and place signal a genuine invitation. For weddings and formal events, a printed or digital invitation with an RSVP is serious.

For weddings, hosts need headcounts for the banquet, so reply clearly and early; not showing after confirming causes real cost and loss of face. For casual meals, a same-day confirmation message is common.
Being invited repeatedly to decline can feel impolite; if you truly can't attend, suggest an alternative date rather than a flat no.
invitations-rsvp.tip: Treat wedding RSVPs firmly; for casual meals, confirm the time the same day.

phrases.en: When is it convenient for you?

phrases.py: Nà tiān bù xíng, gǎi tiān hǎo ma?
phrases.en: How about another day if that day doesn't work?

punctuality.title: Punctuality · 守时
punctuality.subtitle: On time for business, flexible for social.
body: For business meetings, appointments and formal events, punctuality matters — arriving five to ten minutes early is ideal, and lateness requires an apology and a message. Traffic in big cities is unpredictable, so build in buffer time.

For casual social gatherings, timing is looser: arriving a few minutes after the stated time for a meal at someone's home is normal and can even give the host a moment to finish. Large banquets may start a little late as guests trickle in.
Group outings with friends often involve a loose meeting window, but trains, planes, doctor visits and ticketed events run strictly on time — arrive early for those.
punctuality.tip: Be early for business and transport; a few minutes late is acceptable for casual home meals.

phrases.en: I might be ten minutes late.

business-meeting.title: Business Meetings · 商务会议
business-meeting.subtitle: Punctuality, hierarchy and the soft 'no'.
body: Chinese business meetings value punctuality, preparation and hierarchy. Arrive a few minutes early, bring printed materials and business cards, and let the most senior person lead introductions and speak first on each side.

Meetings often open with small talk and tea before business begins — rushing straight to terms can feel abrupt. Disagreement is usually expressed indirectly to preserve harmony and face; a blunt public 'no' is rare, so listen for softer signals like 'we'll study it' (我们再研究研究).

Decisions may take several rounds and often require approval above the room, so patience and relationship-building matter more than forcing a conclusion on the spot. A polite send-off and a thank-you message afterward are standard.
business-meeting.tip: Arrive early, exchange cards with two hands, and read indirect replies as careful rather than weak.

phrases.en: Let's look into it some more.
This is generally acceptable in principle.
It's been a pleasure working with you!

numbers-daily.title: Numbers in Daily Life · 数字吉凶
numbers-daily.subtitle: Lucky 8 and 6, unlucky 4.
body: Numbers carry luck through sound: 8 (bā) resembles 发 (fā, prosper), so phone numbers, license plates and floors rich in 8 cost more; 6 (liù) suggests smoothness (六六大顺); 9 (jiǔ) echoes 久, long-lasting.
The number 4 (sì) sounds like 死 (sǐ, death), so many buildings skip floors 4, 14 and 24, hospitals avoid room 4, and gifts or prices rarely use it. This explains 'missing' buttons in elevators.
Couples love 520 (sounds like 我爱你, I love you) and 1314 (一生一世, a whole lifetime), used in gifts and messages. Knowing these adds charm — and explains the prices.
numbers-daily.tip: Favor 6, 8 and 9; avoid 4 in gifts, room requests and lucky-money amounts.

phrases.en: This building doesn't have a fourth floor.

phrases.py: Wǔ'èr líng dàibiǎo wǒ ài nǐ.

colors-meaning.title: Colors & Their Meanings · 颜色寓意
colors-meaning.subtitle: Red for joy, white for mourning.
body: Red is the color of luck, joy and celebration — weddings, Spring Festival, red envelopes and grand openings all use it. Gold and yellow signal wealth and, historically, the emperor.

White traditionally symbolized mourning (funerals are 'white affairs'), though modern brides also wear white gowns. Black is somber and formal; green is generally positive, but a green hat on a man is a joke implying infidelity — never gift one.
Avoid writing people's names in red ink, which historically signaled a severed relationship or a sentence; use blue or black for names and cards.
colors-meaning.tip: Use red and gold for celebration; never give a man a green hat or write names in red.

feng-shui.title: Feng Shui · 风水
feng-shui.subtitle: Arranging space for good energy.
body: Feng shui (风水) is the traditional art of arranging buildings, doors, furniture and even graves so that energy (气, qì) flows favorably, affecting health, wealth and luck. Many Chinese consider it when choosing a home, office or shop entrance.

Common practices include avoiding a door or bed aligned directly with another, keeping the entrance clear and bright, placing mirrors thoughtfully, and favoring water features and rounded leaves near where money changes hands.

You may notice lucky cats waving in shops, coins and cabbage ornaments, and specific opening dates for businesses. You don't need to believe in it, but respect that many people make real decisions using it.
feng-shui.tip: Don't dismiss feng shui arrangements in a home or shop; they reflect genuine beliefs about luck.

phrases.en: May wealth and treasures come your way.

luck-fortune.title: Luck & Fortune · 福气运气
luck-fortune.subtitle: Fu, luck and the way life unfolds.
body: The idea of 福 (fú, blessing/fortune) runs through daily life — good health, a united family, enough to eat and children who do well are all forms of 福. Wishing someone 福气 is wishing them a blessed, contented life.
Alongside hard work, many Chinese acknowledge 运气 (yùnqi, luck) in exams, business and timing, and use charms, lucky colors and auspicious dates to invite good fortune without relying solely on them.
The character 福 appears on doors, jewelry and decorations; the common phrase 五福临门 wishes five blessings on a household. It's a warm, everyday blessing rather than formal religion.
luck-fortune.tip: Wishing people 福气 or 好运 (good luck) is always welcome, especially at New Year.

phrases.en: May the five blessings come to your home.
Wishing you a share of the joy.

everyday-superstitions.title: Everyday Superstitions · 日常讲究
everyday-superstitions.subtitle: Small habits for avoiding bad luck.
body: Many everyday 'rules' are followed lightly rather than devoutly: don't wash your hair on New Year's Day (you might wash luck away), avoid pointing at the moon as a child, and don't stick chopsticks upright in rice.

Breaking a bowl on a festive day is defused with the phrase 岁岁平安 ('peace year after year'), a pun because 岁 (year) sounds like 碎 (broken). Opening an umbrella indoors and leaving hats on beds are also quietly avoided by some.
Younger Chinese often treat these as old habits or family quirks rather than firm beliefs, but elders may take them seriously — follow along in someone's home out of respect.
everyday-superstitions.tip: Treat these customs lightly and respectfully, especially around elders during festivals.

phrases.en: Wishing you peace and safety year after year!
The elderly are more particular about these things.

face-work.title: Face & Connections at Work · 面子关系
face-work.subtitle: How dignity and networks shape business.
body: Face (面子) and relationships (关系) operate strongly at work. Publicly praising colleagues gives face; openly criticizing someone in a meeting makes them lose face and often backfires, hardening rather than fixing the problem.

Feedback is best delivered gently and in private with a path forward. Building trust through meals, small favors and reliability (人情) smooths approvals and cooperation that formal emails alone cannot.
Status and title matter: address people by surname plus title (王总, 李经理), introduce the most senior person first, and let senior attendees speak before juniors in formal settings.
face-work.tip: Praise in public, correct in private, and invest in relationships before pushing for decisions.

phrases.py: Zhè shì hái qǐng duō guānzhào.
phrases.en: Please give this matter your special attention.

confucian-values.title: Confucian Values · 儒家观念
confucian-values.subtitle: Respect, hierarchy and education.
body: Confucian ideas still shape daily behavior: respect for elders and teachers (孝, xiào; 尊师重道), the value of education and effort, filial duties to family, and knowing one's place within relationships and hierarchy.
Teachers (老师) command great respect, and parents often invest heavily in children's education. Younger people may pour tea for elders, greet them first, and defer to their views in family decisions.
The emphasis on hard work shows in phrases like 吃苦耐劳 (endure hardship and work hard). Understanding this helps explain the strong focus on schooling, exams and family obligations you'll observe.
confucian-values.tip: Greet elders and teachers first and defer to them; education is taken very seriously.

phrases.en: Respect teachers and value the way of learning.
Filial piety is the foundation of all virtues.

harmony-moderation.title: Harmony & Moderation · 中庸和谐
harmony-moderation.subtitle: Valuing balance over confrontation.
body: A deep cultural ideal is harmony (和, hé) and the 'doctrine of the mean' (中庸) — avoiding extremes, keeping balance, and not standing out too sharply. The saying 枪打出头鸟 ('the gun hits the bird that sticks out') reflects caution about being the loudest dissenting voice.
This favors indirect communication, group consensus and compromise. Open conflict, loud arguments and forcing someone into a corner are seen as losing self-control and damaging the group.
It doesn't mean no disagreement exists; rather, it's expressed subtly to preserve the relationship. Patient, balanced framing will usually get you further than confrontation.
harmony-moderation.tip: Seek balance and save face for everyone; frame disagreements as shared problems to solve together.

phrases.en: Each side takes a step back.

tcm-wellness.title: TCM & Wellness · 中医养生
tcm-wellness.subtitle: Hot water, balance and seasonal care.
body: Traditional Chinese medicine (中医) frames health as balance — of yin and yang, hot and cold, and the flow of qì — rather than only treating symptoms. Many everyday habits come from it: drinking warm water, wearing layers to keep the belly warm, and eating foods suited to the season.

After giving birth, women traditionally 'sit the month' (坐月子) with warm foods and rest; in summer people may avoid 'cold-nature' foods like watermelon or iced drinks when feeling unwell. Herbal teas, ginger and goji berries are common.
TCM coexists with modern medicine, and many Chinese use both. Respect the beliefs around it, but for serious illness rely on qualified medical care rather than folk remedies alone.
tcm-wellness.tip: You'll hear food described as 'hot' or 'cold' in nature — it's about balance, not temperature.

phrases.en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do, and pay attention to health preservation.

prayer-incense.title: Praying & Incense · 烧香祈福
prayer-incense.subtitle: How people make wishes at temples.
body: At Buddhist and Daoist temples, worshippers commonly light three sticks of incense, hold them at forehead height, bow toward the main directions, and place them in the burner before praying or making a wish (祈福).

Some people toss crescent-shaped wooden blocks (筊) to ask a deity's answer, tie wish ribbons, or hang prayer locks. Around exam season, families pray at temples dedicated to scholars for students' success.

You may watch respectfully without taking part. Don't blow out incense (wave it out instead), step over burners, or photograph people mid-prayer. Temples are also cultural sites, but they remain active places of belief.
prayer-incense.tip: Observe quietly, don't blow out incense, and avoid photographing worshippers.

phrases.en: Bless us with safety and peace.

metro-etiquette.title: Metro Etiquette · 地铁礼仪
metro-etiquette.subtitle: Riding the world's busiest subways.
body: Chinese metro systems are vast, clean and efficient. Queue behind the platform markings, let passengers exit before boarding (先下后上), and offer seats near the doors to elderly, pregnant or disabled riders — priority seats are clearly marked.

Calls and loud video audio are discouraged, and many cities play reminders to give up seats and keep voices down. Bags go through security X-ray scanners at entrances, and you carry water bottles through.
Pay by tapping a transport card, a phone QR code, or increasingly by tapping a bank card or phone wallet. Rush hour (roughly 7–9 a.m. and 5–7 p.m.) is intensely crowded; avoid it if you can.
metro-etiquette.tip: Let riders out first, offer priority seats, keep audio quiet, and scan bags at security.

phrases.en: Let passengers get off first before boarding.

phrases.py: Qǐng gěi xūyào de rén ràngzuò.
phrases.en: Please give your seat to those in need.

high-speed-rail.title: High-Speed Rail · 高铁
high-speed-rail.subtitle: Fast trains that tie the country together.
body: China's high-speed rail (高铁) network reaches most major cities at up to 350 km/h, often faster and more central than flying. Tickets are real-name, so carry your passport; book via the official app, station machines or counters, and arrive with time for ID and security checks.

Trains are labeled G (fastest), D and C. Carriages and seats are numbered; second class is comfortable, first class roomier. Gates close a few minutes before departure, and large stations can require long walks — arrive 30–45 minutes early.
On board there's hot water, clean toilets, a food trolley and Wi-Fi (often patchy). Keep your ticket and passport handy; you may scan your passport or an ID through the gates.
high-speed-rail.tip: Book with your passport, arrive early in big stations, and note G/D/C train speeds.

phrases.zh: 我要一张去上海的高铁票。
phrases.py: Wǒ yào yī zhāng qù Shànghǎi de gāotiěpiào.
phrases.en: I need a high-speed train ticket to Shanghai.
What time does the ticket check start?

ride-hailing.title: Ride-Hailing & Taxis · 打车
ride-hailing.subtitle: App cars vs street taxis.
body: Ride-hailing apps (网约车, the main one being DiDi) are the easiest way to get around: set pickup and destination on the map, see the fixed fare, and the driver follows GPS — minimal Chinese needed. You can enter the destination in English or show the Chinese address.

Street taxis use meters in cities; sit in the back is common, and payment is by QR or cash. Address drivers politely as 师傅 (shīfu). At stations and airports use the official taxi queue rather than unlicensed touts.
Confirm the license plate in the app matches the car before getting in, and share your trip with someone if traveling alone at night.
ride-hailing.tip: Prefer the official ride-hailing app; verify the plate before entering and use licensed taxi queues.

phrases.en: Driver, I'm going to this address.
What's the last digit of your license plate number?

shared-bikes.title: Shared Bikes · 共享单车
shared-bikes.subtitle: Scan and ride, leave it anywhere.
body: Dockless shared bikes (共享单车) from Meituan and Hellobike blanket cities; scan the QR code on the lock with the relevant app to unlock, ride for a small per-minute fee, and park neatly in a designated bike area when done.

They're ideal for short hops and the 'last mile' from metro stations. Ride with traffic, use bike lanes where available, and wear a helmet on electric bikes. Don't ride two on a standard bike or on pedestrian bridges.
Lock the bike manually in the app or by closing the lock; the app ends the trip. Parking randomly in doorways or on wheelchair ramps draws fines and blocks paths, so use the marked zones.
shared-bikes.tip: Scan to unlock, ride in bike lanes, and park in marked zones then confirm the trip ended.

phrases.en: Scan a bike to rent it.
Is it okay to park here?

public-toilets.title: Public Toilets · 公共厕所
public-toilets.subtitle: Squat toilets and carrying paper.
body: Public toilets in China are increasingly free and clean, especially in malls, stations and newer facilities, but many older or roadside ones are squat-style rather than seated, and free toilet paper is not always provided.
Carry a small pack of tissues and hand sanitizer; this single habit makes travel far easier. Toilets are often marked 男 (men) and 女 (women), with accessible/family stalls sometimes available.
Don't flush paper where a small waste bin is provided beside older toilets, as pipes can be narrow. Modern mall and hotel toilets are fully Western-style.
public-toilets.tip: Carry tissues and sanitizer; read 男/女 for men/women and use the bin for paper where provided.

drinking-water.title: Drinking Water · 自来水
drinking-water.subtitle: Why tap water isn't drunk directly.
body: Tap water in mainland China is generally not safe to drink straight from the faucet, even in big cities; locals boil it or drink bottled or filtered water. Hotels and trains provide hot-water dispensers, and restaurants serve hot water or tea.

Buy cheap bottled water everywhere, or use a refillable bottle with a built-in filter and fill from hot/cooled water dispensers. Ice in drinks at established cafes and chain restaurants is usually made from filtered water.
Brushing teeth with tap water is generally fine in cities, but if you have a sensitive stomach, use bottled or boiled water, especially in rural areas.
drinking-water.tip: Drink bottled, boiled or filtered water; refill from the ubiquitous hot-water dispensers.

phrases.en: A bottle of mineral water, please.
The tap water needs to be boiled.

umbrellas.title: Carrying an Umbrella · 带伞
umbrellas.subtitle: Sun and rain, all year.
body: Chinese city dwellers commonly carry an umbrella year-round — for sudden rain in the south and, especially among women, as a parasol against strong summer sun, since fair skin is traditionally considered attractive.

UV-protection umbrellas are sold everywhere and used on bright days even when it isn't raining; don't be surprised to see them on cloudless summer afternoons. Compact umbrellas are cheap at convenience stores.
Check the weather app before heading out; southern cities and the plum-rain season can bring repeated downpours, and shared umbrellas may not be available when you need one.
umbrellas.tip: Carry a compact umbrella; it serves for both sudden rain and strong sun.

phrases.en: Is it going to rain today?

phrases.py: Tàiyáng zhēn dà, dǎ gè sǎn.
phrases.en: The sun is so strong. I'll use an umbrella.

scenic-booking.title: Booking Scenic Spots · 景点预约
scenic-booking.subtitle: Reserve tickets and slots in advance.
body: Many major museums, palaces and popular scenic spots now require real-name advance reservation (预约) online, sometimes days ahead, with daily visitor caps. The Palace Museum in Beijing, for example, sells out quickly and often has no on-site tickets.
Book through the official WeChat mini-program or app using your passport number, and bring the passport to scan at entry. Some museums are free but still require a reserved slot.
Visit on weekdays and off-season for fewer crowds; holidays and Golden Weeks mean hours-long lines even with tickets.
scenic-booking.tip: Reserve major museums and sights online in advance with your passport, and carry it to enter.

phrases.en: Do I need to make a reservation in advance?

phrases.py: Wǒ yùyuē le, zhè shì zhèngjiàn.
