phrases.en: I have a reservation. Here is my ID.

phrases.py: Jīntiān de piào yuē mǎn le.

peak-crowds.title: Peak Crowds · 人潮
peak-crowds.subtitle: Reading China's crowd calendar.
body: Crowding follows the holiday calendar: Spring Festival, National Day Golden Week and Labor Day see hundreds of millions traveling, so famous sights, trains and highways are packed, sometimes for hours.

Smart travelers either book far in advance and embrace the energy, or explore their own city and visit major sights on ordinary weekdays. The phrase 人山人海 ('people mountain, people sea') captures it vividly.
At crowded events keep your belongings in front pockets, agree on a meeting point if in a group, carry children's contact info, and follow staff and exit signs.
peak-crowds.tip: Avoid top sights during Golden Weeks; if you go, guard belongings and set a meeting point.

hotel-checkin.title: Check-in & ID Cards · 入住证件
hotel-checkin.subtitle: Why you must show a passport.
body: Hotels in China are legally required to register every guest's identity at check-in. Foreigners must show their passport (and sometimes the visa or entry stamp); Chinese guests show their national ID card. Photocopies or photos usually aren't accepted — you need the physical passport.

Not every small hotel is licensed to host foreigners, especially in remote areas; look for places that explicitly accept international guests when booking. Budget chains and international hotels almost always do.
Your details are sent to the public-security system, which is routine. Keep your passport accessible when you travel rather than packed deep in luggage.
hotel-checkin.tip: Carry your physical passport for hotel check-in and choose hotels licensed for foreigners.

greetings-beyond-hello.title: Greetings Beyond Hello · 问候方式
greetings-beyond-hello.subtitle: 'Have you eaten?' and other warm lines.
body: Chinese greetings often sound like personal questions but are simply warm small talk: 你吃了吗? ('Have you eaten?'), 去哪儿啊? ('Where are you off to?'), and 最近忙吗? ('Been busy lately?'). They don't require a detailed answer.
Reply warmly and briefly: 吃了，你呢? ('Yes, and you?'), 出去一下 ('just heading out'), or 还行，不忙 ('not bad, not too busy'). Time-based greetings 早上好/下午好/晚上好 are also standard.
Among neighbors and regular shopkeepers, these daily greetings build familiarity. Answering with a friendly smile is more important than grammatical perfection.
greetings-beyond-hello.tip: Treat 'have you eaten?' and 'where are you going?' as hellos, not real questions.

phrases.en: I'm going out for a bit.

kinship-terms.title: Kinship Terms · 亲属称谓
kinship-terms.subtitle: A word for every relative.
body: Chinese has far more specific family terms than English: 爷爷/奶奶 (paternal grandparents), 外公/外婆 (maternal), 哥哥/弟弟 (older/younger brother), 姐姐/妹妹 (older/younger sister), 叔叔/阿姨 (uncle/aunt), and many cousins distinguished by side and age.
Age order matters, so there's no single generic 'brother' or 'sister' — whether someone is older or younger changes the word. Children learn these from early childhood.
Adults also use kinship words politely for non-relatives: a friendly shopkeeper may be called 阿姨 or 叔叔, an older male worker 师傅, and a young woman 小姐姐 in casual service settings.
kinship-terms.tip: Learn whether a sibling/cousin is older or younger — it changes the Chinese word.

phrases.py: Tā bǐ wǒ dà liǎng suì.
phrases.en: He is two years older than me.

polite-set-phrases.title: Polite Set Phrases · 客气话
polite-set-phrases.subtitle: Fixed lines that smooth daily life.
body: A handful of fixed phrases covers most polite moments: 请问 (may I ask) before questions, 不好意思 (excuse me/sorry) for light apologies and getting attention, 麻烦你 (sorry to trouble you) when asking a favor, and 辛苦了 (thanks for your hard work) to staff and drivers.
Responses are equally formulaic: 不客气/不谢 (you're welcome), 没关系 (it's fine), and 应该的 (it's only right). Learning these call-and-response pairs makes interactions flow naturally.
Politeness in Chinese often uses 您 (polite 'you') for elders and strangers, and softening words like 一下 ('a bit') to make requests less direct: 等一下, 帮我一下.
polite-set-phrases.tip: Lead questions with 请问, use 不好意思 to get attention, and answer thanks with 不客气.

phrases.en: Excuse me, how do I get there?
Thank you for your hard work!

responding-compliments.title: Responding to Compliments · 谦虚回应
responding-compliments.subtitle: Deflect praise rather than accept it.
body: Unlike the English 'thank you', Chinese convention often deflects compliments modestly to avoid seeming proud: 哪里哪里 ('not at all'), 没有没有 ('no, no'), 过奖了 ('you flatter me'), or 还差得远呢 ('far from it').
This modesty is expected even when you're genuinely skilled; a direct 'yes, I know I'm good' can sound arrogant. You can then return the compliment: 你也很棒 ('you're great too').
Younger Chinese in casual settings may simply say 谢谢, especially in international companies, so both patterns work — but modest deflection is the safe, traditional choice with elders.
responding-compliments.tip: Deflect praise with 哪里哪里 or 过奖了, then return a kind word.

phrases.py: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de zhēn hǎo!
Nǎlǐ nǎlǐ, hái chà dé yuǎn.
phrases.en: Not at all, I'm still far from good.
You're too kind. / Thank you, but I'm not that great.

chengyu-four-char.title: Four-Character Idioms · 成语
chengyu-four-char.subtitle: Compact wisdom in four characters.
body: 成语 (chéngyǔ) are set phrases, almost always four characters, often drawn from ancient stories that educated Chinese instantly recognize. Used well, they make speech vivid and show real cultural fluency.
Common examples: 人山人海 (a sea of people), 入乡随俗 (when in Rome), 马马虎虎 (so-so), 一举两得 (kill two birds with one stone), 守株待兔 (trust blindly to luck), and 画蛇添足 (gild the lily / overdo it).
Because each packs a back-story, learn the meaning and the right context, not just the literal characters; dropping one in at a fitting moment charms native speakers.
chengyu-four-char.tip: Use a well-placed 成语 for charm, but only when you're sure of the context.

phrases.en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

internet-slang.title: Internet Slang · 网络流行语
internet-slang.subtitle: How young Chinese type and joke.
body: Chinese internet slang moves fast and often uses number puns and abbreviations: 520 (I love you), 666 (liùliùliù, 'awesome/smooth'), 88 (bābā, sounds like 'bye-bye'), and 996 (the grueling 9-to-9, six-days work schedule).

Common phrases include 加油 ('add oil' = go for it), 躺平 ('lie flat' = opt out of the grind), 内卷 (involution, rat-race competition), 绝绝子 (absolutely amazing), and 卖萌 (acting cute). Emojis and stickers often replace words in chat.
Slang is informal and generational — fun with friends your age, but avoid it in formal work messages or with elders, where standard polite Chinese is expected.
internet-slang.tip: Use slang only with peers; 666 means 'awesome', 88 means 'bye', and 加油 means 'go for it'.

phrases.en: Come on, you can do it!

dialects-accents.title: Dialects & Accents · 方言口音
dialects-accents.subtitle: One written language, many spoken ones.
body: China has many spoken dialects and language groups — Mandarin (普通话), Cantonese (粤语), Shanghainese (吴语), Hokkien/Min, Hakka and more — some mutually unintelligible. Standard Mandarin, based on the Beijing accent, is taught nationwide and binds the country.

Thanks to universal schooling and media, almost everyone under a certain age speaks Mandarin, though regional accents are strong, especially in the south and southeast. Older people in some areas may speak little Mandarin.

You're learning Mandarin, which works everywhere. In Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau, Cantonese is the lively local tongue; hearing the same written characters spoken completely differently is normal, not a mistake.
dialects-accents.tip: Learn standard Mandarin for nationwide use; treat Cantonese and others as distinct spoken languages.

phrases.py: Wǒ tīng bù tài dǒng fāngyán.

characters-writing.title: Characters & Writing · 汉字书写
characters-writing.subtitle: Strokes, radicals and typing.
body: Chinese characters (汉字) combine meaning and sound; many contain a 'radical' hinting at meaning (water 氵, person 亻, hand 扌) and a component hinting at pronunciation. Stroke order follows set rules and is taught from childhood.

Most Chinese now 'write' on phones by typing pinyin and selecting characters, so handwriting ability has declined even among natives — but recognizing characters and understanding radicals speeds up reading and dictionary use enormously.

As a learner, focus first on pinyin and recognition, then practice writing high-frequency characters; apps and tracing the stroke order help. Typing pinyin is how you'll actually input Chinese in daily life.
characters-writing.tip: Learn radicals to guess meaning and type via pinyin; handwriting comes gradually.

phrases.en: How do you write this character?

phrases.py: Sāndiǎnshuǐ de zì hé shuǐ yǒuguān.
phrases.en: Characters with the 'three drops of water' radical are related to water.

choosing-names.title: Choosing a Chinese Name · 取中文名
choosing-names.subtitle: Sound, meaning and lucky characters.
body: Chinese names are usually two or three characters: a one-character family name followed by a one- or two-character given name chosen for meaning and sound. Parents pick characters for wishes like 明 (bright), 伟 (great), 静 (quiet), 雪 (snow) or 安 (peace).
Names avoid homophones with unlucky words and may be checked for balance of the five elements or stroke counts. Given names can feel quite gendered, though modern choices are increasingly neutral.

If you adopt a Chinese name, pick something that sounds a little like your own name with a positive meaning — a teacher or Chinese friend can help you avoid accidental awkward meanings. Use your real surname or a similar-sounding Chinese one.
choosing-names.tip: Ask a Chinese speaker to check your chosen name for sound, meaning and accidental puns.

phrases.en: Do you have a Chinese name?

chinglish-signs.title: Chinglish & English Signs · 中式英语
chinglish-signs.subtitle: Funny signs and English in daily life.
body: You'll encounter English on signs, menus and packaging that ranges from fluent to charmingly odd — literal translations like 'slip carefully' (wet floor), 'hand-pulled husband lung pieces' (a noodle dish), or poetic but confusing warnings. These are often called Chinglish.

Major cities, airports and international chains use clear standard English, and translation apps handle menus instantly. Older or smaller places may have no English at all, so learning key Chinese phrases pays off.

Amusing signs make great photos, but be kind about them — multilingual China is the norm, and the person who ordered the sign may be proud of it. Learning a little Chinese is warmly appreciated everywhere.
chinglish-signs.tip: Use a translation app for menus; enjoy odd signs with humor and respect.
